title: The motor's frequency response
summary: Read a Bode plot: voltage to speed is a first-order lag whose bandwidth is 1/τ, and voltage to angle is an integrator, which is why a position servo needs no integral term.

steps.title: The time constant
steps.text:
Apply a 12 V step to the motor with no controller and run. The speed rises like 1 − e^(−t/τ), with the mechanical time constant

    τ = J R / (K² + b R)

Read τ in the Summary, and compare it with the time to reach 63 % of the final speed.

check.hint: Load the setup and press Run.
check.success: τ = 0.196 s, and the speed reaches 63 % at 0.195 s: one time constant, as e^(−1) = 0.37 says.

steps.title: Voltage to speed
steps.text:
The Analyze ▸ Bode tab shakes the motor with a sine wave of voltage at every frequency ω and plots how large the speed swing is (gain, in dB) and how far it lags (phase).

It is set to Voltage → Speed. Run, then read the DC gain (the gain for a steady voltage) and the bandwidth (where the gain has fallen 3 dB).

check.hint: Press Run, then choose Voltage → Speed on the Analyze ▸ Bode tab.
check.success: A slow wiggle gets the full 9.8 rad/s per volt, K / (K² + b R). The bandwidth, 5.15 rad/s, is close to 1/τ = 5.10 rad/s: above it the rotor's inertia can't keep up, and the gain falls 20 dB per decade with 90° of lag, like a first-order system. Far above, past the electrical pole at about 395 rad/s (near R/L), the inductance adds another 20 dB per decade and another 90°: that is why the phase ends at −180°.

steps.title: A heavier load
steps.text: Double the inertia J to 0.002 kg·m² (a heavier load on the shaft) and run again. What should happen to τ, and to the bandwidth?

check.hint: Press Run, and keep Voltage → Speed on the Analyze ▸ Bode tab.
check.success: τ doubles to 0.39 s and the bandwidth halves to about 2.6 rad/s. The low-frequency gain stays 9.8: inertia only matters while the speed is changing.

steps.title: Voltage to angle
steps.text: Now look at the shaft angle instead of the speed. The setup puts J back and shows Voltage → Angle. Run, and look at the left end of the gain curve.

check.hint: Press Run, then choose Voltage → Angle on the Analyze ▸ Bode tab.
check.success: The DC gain is infinite: the angle is the integral of the speed, so a steady voltage turns the shaft forever. The gain climbs 20 dB for every decade lower in ω, the phase starts at −90°, and above 1/τ (about 5 rad/s) the gain falls 40 dB per decade.

steps.title: Why P control holds an angle
steps.text: In the position servo ("Position PD" preset), the controller has no integral term, yet the shaft ends exactly on the target angle. Why?

options: The motor already integrates speed into angle, so any steady error would keep the shaft turning until the error is gone
The bandwidth is high enough to remove any error
The inductance L stores the error and cancels it
check.hint: What did the infinite DC gain of Voltage → Angle tell you?
check.success: The plant's integrator does the integral term's job for a step in the target. Add a steady load torque, though, and a P or PD loop is left with an error: then the controller needs its own Ki (see the "Load torque disturbance" preset).
